text: Working with Dreams in a Clinical Setting HERMA REESKAMP, M.D. A disturbed sleep pattern, nightmares, and anxiety-filled dreams form a cluster of symptoms belonging to the DSM- IV diagnosis of Post-traumatic Stress Disorder. A psychotherapeutic group approach aimed at reducing these symptoms was undertaken in the form of a workshop. The workshop was not a regular part of the treatment program, but an experimental endeavor, offered to the patients during special occasions in the year (around holidays). The therapist was primarily interested in investigating possibilities for improving the quality of sleep and infiuencing the patterns of recurring anxiety-filled dreams and nightmares. The method has both structured and psychodynamic elements. The work carried out during the dream group was embedded in the total treatment program. This was crucial to allow personal themes to be continued in the regular treatment program. INTRODUCTION A disturbed sleep pattern, nightmares, and anxiety-filled dreams form a cluster of symptoms belonging to the DSM-IV (APA, 1994) diagnosis of Post Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD). These symptoms are difficult to influence and throughout a patient's lifetime, often return after temporary improvement or seem resistant to change altogether. Patients tend to use avoidance techniques to postpone going to sleep at night or they avoid talking about their traumatic experiences, fearing they will stir up bad dreams. A psychotherapeutic group approach in the form of a workshop was undertaken to stimulate patients from our in-patient clinic to approach their dreams in a new, more active and creative way. The workshop was intended to help patients change the haunting themes of their nightmares and anxiety-filled dreams. The workshop was not a regular part of the treatment program, but an experimental endeavor offered to the patients during special occasions in the year (around holidays). The clinic offers Centrum '45, Oegstgeest, the Netherlands. Mailing address: Rijnzichtweg 35,2342 AX Oegstgeest, The Netherlands, e-mail: h.reeskamp@centrum45.nl AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PSYCHOTHERAPY, Vol. 60, No. 1, 2006 23 AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PSYCHOTHERAPY programs on a 24-hour schedule from Sunday evening to Friday afternoon. The staff consists of sociotherapists on the ward, a social worker, a nurse, a creative therapist, a psychomotor therapist, and three individual-and group psychotherapists, one of whom is a psychiatrist and the head of the clinic. This article is not meant to describe this treatment in total. It focuses on an experimental and new initiative. It may be of interest to note that the therapists who facilitated the dream workshops are also the clinic's regular psychotherapists, only working in a different role during the workshop. While the work itself was instigated and carried out by the author, helped by one other psychotherapist in the actual carrying out of the workshop, the clinic's other team members had to deal with the material instigated, as one therapy always flows over into the others in a clinic. The principal motivation in working with dreams in this way was based on psychoanalytic interest; the activation of the creative unconscious in helping patients overcome rigidity in their self-perception. Rigid concep- tualisation and repetition phenomena, in persisting nightmares and anxiety dreams can be considered an aspect of fixation in the flow of ongoing development throughout a lifetime. The patient population of the CENTRUM '45, Dutch national centre for the treatment of war-related traumas, is heterogeneous: first- and second-generation traumatized victims of World War II (WWII) and veterans of WWII and more recent wars. Some patients, such as journalists or professional health care workers, were traumatized through their work in war circumstances. The age range of the population falls between thirty and eighty years. Those in the so called second generation have not been in war-related life circumstances, but have grown up in a family with parents and/or older siblings who were traumatized, became seriously iU, or had died because of the war. This heterogeneity of our patients requires that we offer a type of psychotherapy that is not typical for the treatment of specific symptoms. By and large, the tradition in the institute is psychoanalytic group psycho- therapy, varying from insight-oriented to mainly supportive treatment. The other theoretical orientations prevailing among the psychotherapists offer- ing individual psychotherapy are either psychoanalytic or client centered. Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing sessions have been tried (Shapiro, 2001) and elements of behavior therapy, such as registration, were applied. Systematic desensitization was not undertaken. A new initiative to treat patients in a group format with imagery rehearsal (Krakow, Kellner, Neidhardt, Pathak & Lambert, 1993) is about to start. 24 Working with Dreams in a Clinical Setting In the workshop model different elements, such as joumal keeping and structured/non-structured group psychotherapy, were applied. For four weeks prior to the workshop we asked patients to record their sleep patterns and write down their dreams in a daily journal. The daily journal was part of the Nocturnal Intrusions after Traumatic Experiences ques- tionnaire (NITE) (Schreuder, Kleijn & Rooijmans, 2000). After collecting the journal forms each week, the therapist read and categorized the recorded dreams. The first category contained anxiety-filled dreams and nightmares, the second category contained dreams that seemed to rework other themes and events not specifically trauma related. A third category went beyond the first two because it contained dreams with special symbols. Among these were certain more universal types of dreams, such as finding a forgotten or neglected baby, or saving one, and dreams about flying, floods of water or fires. It was immediately clear to the dreamers that these dreams were no work out of old themes or memories. Symbolic language was predominant. After reviewing the journals, the therapist began to observe recurring themes, themes of moving on, or of new elements appearing in the dreams at the end of several weeks. The themes that emerged were quite interest- ing, especially for the patients who complained of having recurring night- mares. The workshop offered patients the possibility to explore new ways of perceiving and experiencing dreams and the ability to reinvestigate attri- butions on both cognitive and emotional levels. This allowed for new openings in which the fixated meaning of the dreams could be trans- formed. During individual psychotherapy sessions, many patients reported having nightmares that replicated traumatic events, but on closer inspec- tion the dreams were often very symbolic and in no way typical replicas of some past traumatic experience. In this experimental endeavor, there is no difference in psychothera- peutic approach between this group of patients and any other category of patients suffering from psychic distress. Theoretically, the author presup- poses that a person can be distressed by a great many causes, such as a world war impinging on the inner balance, chronic piling up of distressing factors in a family, or any mix of these two factors. To improve the health of our patients, however, it seemed wise to appeal to universal principles that many psychotherapeutic schools have objectified: to generate hope and to appeal to novelty seeking interests. Many traumatized patients reduce their scope of vision by repeating only the negative events in their 25 AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PSYCHOTHERAPY lives. And therapists, out of respect for the overwhelming historic events these patients have survived, can be tempted to go along without ques- tioning the rightness of the patients' perceptions, Laub and Auerhahn (1993) described the stages in which traumatic memory can be organized. The stages are: not knowing, fugue states, fragments, transference phenomena, overpowering narratives, life themes, witnessed narratives, and metaphors. Memory content changes depending on the degree of dissociation and repression. There is a relationship between integration during therapy and the use of reflection and change in the attribution of meaning. The final stage of memory, as a metaphor, offers the possibility to transform trauma, to loosen up the rigidity of perception by investigating and even creating (constructing) new meaning. The objective in the dream workshop was to use group dynamic forces to loosen up the rigid perceptions of dreams held by the individual patients, A psychodynamic group process furthers a diffusion of the ego boundaries and thereby allows a temporary regression to the pre-oedipal and preverbal stages of development (Debbane & Lamoureux, 1997; Bienvenue, Debane, de Carufel and Piper, 1986). In group-therapeutic language, the level of functioning of the individ- ual group members, because of the deepening of the regression, has been designated as a primordial state of mind, (Foulkes, 1964, Usandivaras, 1985, Zanasi, 1996). In individual psychotherapy, intrapsychic contents can remain more integrated and can be cognitively interpreted and per- ceived by the patient. In a psychodynamic group these contents spread out in projections on the group as a whole (Bion, 1959). Contributions by the individual group members take on the quality of part objects from the individual patient. When the patient eventually reintegrates this spread out contents of his own psyche, these are influenced, enriched, and changed. These theoretical concepts were the basis of undertaking the dream workshop that the author believed would help our patients overcome the nightly repetition of fear and suffering. The last case study in this paper illustrates how a shift in a patient's perception took place and how the patient recognized the nightmare as a repetition phenomenon that was based on an internal psychic conflict concerning long-repressed feelings of shame and guUt over his own aggressive deeds. The nightmare about civil war-like events seemed to have been a persisting mental structure, a screen to ward off his inner conflicting psychic contents (Lansky, 1995). 26 Working with Dreams in a Clinical Setting THE ORGANISATION OF THE WORKSHOP The first workshop was offered to patients on a voluntary basis, as part of a special Christmas program. Very anxious patients had the option not to participate if they feared their situation would decompensate because they might experience more bad dreams. Patients could take part in another type of psychodrama workshop, dealing with situations in the family of origin, offered at the same time as the dream workshop. Fifteen of the 24 patients we invited to participate chose to take part in the dream workshop. After reviewing all of the patients' journal entries from the preceding four weeks, the therapist decided to give the workshop the structure of a dream-psychodrama group and to guide the group together with a col- league. Both group psychotherapists have experience in using psychomo- tor and drama techniques. One therapist carried out warming-up exer- cises with the patients and the other directed the dream scenes that were played out. All patients participated in the reenactments of the dreams that were brought in by different patients. In each session, two dreams were reenacted. There were two sessions in total. For one of the dream plays, the patients switched roles and reenacted the dream play. For each play, patients acted, witnessed, and experienced, but no interpretations (on a cognitive level) were offered. Patients discussed their experiences during the dream workshop in the regular therapy sessions and the dream plays were used as actual themes in the regular therapies. The second workshop, some three months later, was meant to be conducted with all of the 24 patients. Patients were divided into two groups that followed two different sessions in sequence. The first session was conducted by a colleague who led the patients through psychomotor exercises. The second session was a group psychotherapeutic one, con- ducted by the author of this article. This time the group psychotherapist used an adaptation of the dream analysis model described by Shuttleworth-Jordan and colleagues (1988), who worked with dreams in a structured manner with outpatient groups. Their model was adapted to fit a clinical setting. Structure, as well as psychodynamic elements, was used in the group psychotherapeutic sessions. We started with a short relaxation exercise, consisting of sitting in a chair, concentrating on breathing, and releasing tensions in different parts of the body. Shutdeworth-Jordan and col- leagues took sufficient time to deeply relax patients by autogenic training, inducing feelings of warmth and weight, and by breathing exercises. 27 AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PSYCHOTHERAPY After relaxation exercises, patients who wished to do so could submit a dream to the group. However, to reduce the tension for very anxious participants, the patients were told they could just listen and take part as they would in the regular group psychotherapy. The following steps were outlined for the patients: 1) One patient would relate a dream to the group; other group members could ask questions to get a clear picture of the dream scenes, persons and circumstances. While Shuttleworth-Jordan and colleagues made use of active imagination to allow everyone in the group to recreate the images of the dream as vividly as possible in their own minds, we did not introduce active imagination as a separate method, but used the group dynamic described in the next step. 2) Group members (other than the dreamer) could give their personal associations with the dream, without trying to interpret the dream. In the psychodynamic part of the session, in which the dreamer participates, the group grows toward an understanding as connec- tions between each group member's contributions are sensed. Little pieces of interpretation gradually occur. 3) The therapist joins in by summarizing the things that have been said, adding associations or meanings to the symbols, but without giving a final interpretation. Most of the literature on dream groups is about outpatient groups. For this workshop, it seemed best to stick to the model of clinical treatment, where each activity is always embedded in the clinical setting and in the total treatment program. In such a setting, interpretations need not be completed; the growing common understanding can continue to work in the unconscious of the group, enabling future understanding or reinter- pretation. Interpretation is always a construction at a certain moment in time and builds on the confluence of perceptions and associations of a group (Foulkes, 1964). Meaning is already grasped by the group members during the free association part of the session as a more fleeting creation, a temporary gestalt becoming visible. Not interpreting in a way that is too final leaves open the possibility to rework the meaning in the future. The value of the psychoanalytic group is the diversity of observations and the thinking capacity of groups, moving beyond the limits of the individual resistance. The pleasure principle in a group is expressed in a playful way of learning. This principle worked certainly in the first dream group workshop, making use of enactment, rather than verbal interpretation. 28 Working with Dreams in a Clinical Setting A CASE EXAMPLE FROM THE FIRST DREAM GROUP A well-prepared patient recounts the dream she had two nights before the workshop and which she wrote down in her journal, I find myself in a house full of chaos and rubbish. It is a situation that took place long ago, when I was left alone with my children in the house after my divorce. A strange looking man knocks at the window and starts scolding me. I open the door and then realize he has mistaken me for someone else. I tell him he is at the wrong address, talking to the wrong person. Than he quiets down and apologizes. Suddenly three years have passed in the dream and the house is tidied up. Everything is looking new and clean. I walk through the house, very pleased, and open a door in the basement. To my surprise, I find a completely furnished garage, with a brand-new hydraulic lift for cars. I think: "This house contains things I do not need. I never repair cars." The patient comments this was certainly the most surprising discovery in the dream. After her recounting of the dream, the group was able to ask questions to clarify the image of the house, the garage, and the man in the dreamV The group also started asking the patient questions about the period after her divorce. The therapist noticed the group might be ready to proceed to the next step and invited them to continue with the exchange of personal ideas and associations, yet without interpreting the meaning. The patient remembers being in a chaotic frame of mind at the time of her divorce, disrupted in her life, left alone with her children. Questions were asked about the strange man, for whom the patient opened her door. Group members were astonished about the woman not being afraid and some members observed that they would not open the door for such a type of stranger. The patient's dream demonstrated that she could react in a way that was different from her usual way of reacting, as it was perceived before in the clinic (the patient had a pattern of interactions that triggered aggression from others, leaving her feeling threatened, alone, and misun- derstood). One group member thought the dream was showing that something sexual was about to happen because of the presence of the woman and a man, , .then felt embarrassed by the assessment, saying: "This probably has something to do with me, as usual," Yet another group member thought of Santa Claus. Amazement and laughter followed in the group. Yes, he explained, Santa Claus, holding onto a sack can be seen as threatening, but once you know that presents come out of the sack, the perception becomes different and more benign. 29 AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PSYCHOTHERAPY The group members continued to ask questions about the dream: "How did she know three years had gone by in the dream?" The patient responded that this was evident, she just knew, because the house had totally changed, everything was crystal clear, clean, and new. All the rubbish had gone. The image of the garage was quite a surprise to her. Some people asked about her husband: "Was he technical?" "No not al all!" The patient volunteered that her husband was very rational in his profession (as a research psychologist), but he never did any repairs at home, and she always did the repair work. The image of the hydraulic lift for cars was intriguing; it seemed to have something to do with her own capacities to repair, she can do it herself now. The group sensed that the dream was showing the patient something that she had no knowledge of, and the therapist repeats the consensus: there are more possibilities in store for the patient than she realized. The interpretation is near at hand now: apparently this dream, which occurred at the end of the patient's therapy, shows her the changes she went through. Her ability to view the situation has become clear, she can better cope with threatening situations, she became stronger, and she has hidden capacities she did not realize she had. From a psychoanalytic point of view, this patient took back her paranoid projections and so strengthened the basis of her personality. As for the patient who thought the dream was indicating something sexual between a man and a woman—he felt quite wrong now. The therapist remarked that "letting in the man" might be interpreted as the patient regaining her strength and her male side, which also may be symbolized in the hydraulic lift in her garage. At this point in the discussion, the therapist asked the patient if she would recount a dream she had when first beginning therapy. This was a dream about marriage; she and her son passed a richly dressed bride on their way to an unspecified place. The dream ended with both mother and son lying on a bed high up in the sky. The beds were on scaffolding poles. While the son could easily slide down these poles, the woman was desperate, stuck high in the air on the wobbly construction. She thought in her dream: "Only a helicopter can save me now." Comparing the wobbly feeling of this bed construction to the strong hydraulic lift for repairing cars in the basement of her house seemed quite a transformation. The group members concluded that this patient had found a different way of dealing with her emotions. The patient was in the last phase of her treatment, which lasted for a year and a half. 30 Working with Dreams in a Clinical Setting CASE EXAMPLES FROM THE SECOND DREAM GROUP The previous dream can be described as a reworking of old themes. An overview has been given of the total situation of the patient, from past events to future possibilities. The dream gave her direction for her present situation, the end of treatment. This second group of patients consisted of a number of first generation victims of WWII. They brought their persistent nightmares into the workshop. The patient speaking to this group was a first- and second-generation war victim from the Netherlands Indies, who had been in a Japanese concentration camp as a child and grown up in a disrupted family after the war. The patient, a woman in her sixties, claims to have few, if any, memories of her early chUdhood experiences in a concentration camp, and she recounted a nightmare that has repeated itself throughout her whole life. I am in a black hole, no light above. It must be a dark night. I am in some sort of a crater filled with black coal gravel. I try to get a grip on it, but it is gravel and I cannot get a hold of it. I am alone in this place. The dream has continued to reoccur since I was fifteen years of age. I wake up desperate and suffocating. The group began to work in the way the therapist had explained to them, by first asking clarifying questions. They asked about the concen- tration camp, but the dreamer has hardly any memory of it. Then they asked her questions about her family. The patient explained that she grew up in a strict family and social activities were limited. She came from a family with four quiet and obedient little children who, once weekly on Saturday evenings, were allowed to listen to one radio program, after which they drank a cup of warm chocolate. This was the only family activity that she remembers. She tells the group that as an adult even her husband let her down; he never showed concern for her and abandoned her for a younger woman. The group asks for details on the black hole; what exactly does it look like? "Like the very large crater of a volcano," she responds. Then the patient starts to explain why she is at the clinic. She says it is so that she can come out of her loneliness and isolation and learn how to make contact with people because she has never learned to do so. The group remains silent. The patient speaks out about her desire to get out of this isolation, to encounter other people, and to see light somewhere, not as from a hole above, but as if from some horizontal tunnel leading to a light point and 31 AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PSYCHOTHERAPY some exit. As the patient keeps associating, buUding on the images in her dream and trying to imagine a solution, the group listens in silence. Although the patient spoke about listening to a radio program as a child, she could not remember the name. The therapist's associations went to "The Black Hole," the name of a radio program in The Netherlands that focused on the supernatural, the lead in of which was something like this: "There is more under the sun, than our eyes can see and our mind can grasp. ... " The group remained quiet while the therapist continued verbalizing her thoughts in an effort to lead the group to the process of exploration. The image in this patient's dream is archaic, reflecting intense loneli- ness and abandonment. In terms of self-psychology, these images reflect a self-state (Natterson, 1978, Reeskamp, 1997), The images do not point to inner conflicts, as is the case in the neurotic personality, but present containment for the patient. The issues to be contained are fear of death, destruction of the self, the fear of falling apart, getting entirely lost, and disappearing from existence. It is wise not to analyze these images, to search for underlying tensions, but to give an interpretation that strength- ens the ego of the patient: The so-called technique of upward interpreting. The therapist asks: "Did you ever hear of this radio program 'The Black Hole'?" The patient responds that she knows of the program, though she had not listened to it. Nevertheless, the patient seems to understand what the therapist is insinuating. Mental health workers have observed the patient as a person lacking in common sense about how to relate in social situations. They estimate that her personality falls in the so-called asocial personality part of the spectrum. The patient, being very sensitive, expe- riences this opinion as having negative connotations. She believes that she is being judged as being wrong instead of being understood. She had to fight for admission in the clinic, as some psychotherapists, who had been her initial interviewers, feared she could regress after admission. She indeed had a longing to do over things in her life that went wrong. Yet, in her time at the clinic she did not regress or decompensate. Considering all of these aspects in rendering an opinion, the therapist attempts to con- struct a cognitive interpretation of the patient's dream. You grew up in an environment tbat could not react in a normal socially engaging manner because your parents were struggling to survive, you only had yourself. In the midst of terrible circumstances in the concentration camp, you had to develop an inner strength so that you could gain a sense of protection and holding that was not available to you in your family. What you could not grow socially grew in your inner strength. You found strength 32 Working with Dreams in a Clinical Setting in spirituality and supernatural phenomena. It is a basic need to feel secure in the world. All humans need this feeling of safety and belonging. Under normal circumstances this is gained in the family: People that have the opportunity to grow up in a warm nest sometimes will not develop such a strong inner core, as you have done. While the therapist continued with this theme, looking at the dream from various angles, the patient's face lit up. She no longer felt strange as the context was explained for her in terms that built up her individual development. The explanation gave the patient an overview of the total situation, with positive and negative sides of her development highlighted. She felt that her pain has been recognized and her feelings of isolation ameliorated. She was able to regain her own strength and autonomy. The patient closed her portion of the group session by expressing feelings of relief. She was happy with this new view of herself and concluded by saying that therapy will be a learning process for her. She says she will commence on the journey to bring more balance between her own inner world and that of social contacts. Five minutes before the end of the session, another group member reluctantly took his turn. He had hesitated, waiting until the last moment, fearing to burden others with his terrible nightmare. The therapist felt the patient's desire to find answers for the recurring, anxiety-filled dreams he experienced. During the psychodrama workshop, the patient had partially participated by keeping his dream journal, yet he anxiously refused to use any of his dreams as play examples. This patient was an extremely anxious, rigidly controlled person, who always dressed in black, and in the past, had been the leader of a gang. During this part of his life he had used quite a bit of violence. However, he now felt ashamed of that part of his life and did not want to talk about it during the regular therapy groups. He finally came forward with his dream: All my dreams have the same pattern: They start normal and pleasant. During the dream things change and become threatening, it turns into a nightmare: I am persecuted, surrounded, attacked, and killed. Only in one dream, the last one, the script took a different course. This patient had had this different type of dream before the previous workshop, but refused at that time to talk about it in the group. He was too anxious. The therapist encouraged him to take a chance this time. Maybe this dream was more than just a nightmare. . . . l^o, this dream is one of those old dreams: I walked with a friend on a large plane of white sand, like a beach. Suddenly, the beach is full of cackling 33 AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PSYCHOTHERAPY chickens. As we get closer to the chickens we watch a group of Africans with chopping knifes, hacking ever-increasing amounts of chickens that seem to be coming out of the ground. We are frightened of being slaughtered and keep our distance from the scene by walking around it in a large half circle. Then the cackling of the chicken changes into the crying of babies. This is very strange indeed. We stop and look back over our shoulders. Hundreds of children's heads are now coming out of the blood-soaked sand. The children are crying and unprotected. Their heads are being chopped off mercilessly. The patient recalled that he woke up in an anxious state, being very bewildered with the vividness of the horrible scene, and told his dream to the night nurse. He then walked out on the street at four o'clock in the morning, with a kris in his hand (A kris is an Indonesian dagger, believed to possess magical powers to ward off evil. It is handed over only to male family members, and is considered to have individuality and a wiU of its own.) The night nurse gently persuaded him back into the clinic. After he was inside the clinic, he broke into tears and vomited. The patient cannot make sense of this dream. He does not understand anything about the children's heads. The group sits in silence; one patient, who had worked in Africa, sits gazing into space. The clock indicates it is time to end the session. Like a flash of lightning, an observation comes from our previous patient, the woman who had dreamt about the black hole: "This is you!" "You always decapitate new life." The therapist asks if he can recognize a similar theme in a previous dream of his: images of a running brook in a mountain meadow carrying his dead father along. The group now has a sense of acknowledgement of their feelings and starts to pour out associations: water is new life, let go of the control a bit, allow yourself to come into motion. Accept life without needing to slay any new development. The therapist remarked that the children's heads com- ing out of the ground could signify new birth. The session ended with the patient being somewhat confused about these totally different perceptions of the dream (different from his own rigid way of perception). This was enough for him; he needed some time to process all of the feedback from the group. Several weeks later, the patient was still working on under- standing his dream. He requested a private consultation with a therapist. He revealed that he had remembered how he had gotten a girl pregnant and had insisted that she should end the pregnancy, though she wanted to keep the baby. His other aggressive acts were pressuring his conscience now. He felt quite ashamed, but now that he did not need to repress the memory about his aborted child any longer, he decided to open up about 34 Working with Dreams in a Clinical Setting these matters to alleviate his feelings of guilt. (Three years after the workshop and the ensuing working through of these topics, the patient communicated that his anxiety dreams and nightmares had subsided, only once did he have an anxious type of dream.) DISCUSSION The dream group was heterogeneous, consisting of traumatized pa- tients from a variety of backgrounds. This workshop model was shown to be a valuable ingredient in the psychotherapeutic treatment of recurrent nightmares (Schreuder, van Egmond, Kleijn & Visser, 1998). Patients proceeded with other therapies using the themes that were generated in these workshops. In both trials—the first workshop using psychodrama techniques, and the second one, using psychotherapeutic techniques— patients experienced a fresh way of looking at matters. No one seemed to feel bound to the role patterns and loyalties that are usually encountered in regular groups: We found that using a different approach, such as the workshops, appeals to the curiosity, hope, and creativity of the patients. The surprise element in this way of presenting therapeutic work (in contrast to what patients had become used to in the regular program), seemed to be effective. It is understood that a regular program influences patients in important ways as well. There can be no surprise without a regular expectation as its base. The ability to be playful in the associative part of the session was beneficial, freeing patients from their tendency to have a controlled and limited way of reacting. In therapy, this limited attitude is often in the foreground. The desires are kept hidden away in the background. This attitude prohibits having an open perspective and seeing the possibilities in life. It was beneficial for both patients and therapists to take a fresh look at versions of stories that seemed to repeat themselves. These versions could be changed and used in a productive way. All the journals were kept, and used later for research purposes. Some of the research questions were: Does the keeping of a journal itself have a positive influence over time? Does the content of the written dream stories change over time? Is this related to less persistent nightmares and anxiety-fiUed dreams? The individuals described in the case examples seemed to take a positive turn in their therapies. In a separate article, the results of the systematic analysis of the journals, that were kept during an extended period after this workshop will be analyzed. The analysis is carried out by a separate research psychologist and the author. 35 AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PSYCHOTHERAPY Acknowledgment: I thank Tammy Bean, Wim Eeenstra and Wim Kleijn for their corrections and thoughtful comments on earlier versions of this article.
